newsitem.title: USA: Science journal floats outer space April Fool joke.
newsitem.headline: Science journal floats outer space April Fool joke.

text.p: The normally sober-sided journal Science floated an elaborate April Fools' joke on its Web site featuring a bowling-ball-sized meteorite from a Jupiter moon, naked mole rats and the New Jersey Turnpike.

The joke, dated April 1 but still visible at midday Thursday at www.sciencenow.org, bore the headline "Meteorite Hints at Life on Jupiter Moon" and said the space rock from Jupiter's satellite Europa showed signs of microbial life.

Even for those who monitor astronomy news, this was not an automatic red flag, since NASA's Galileo space probe has been surveying Europa and scientists reported in January that Europa might be hospitable to life.

The first clue that the story might not be all it seemed was the alleged location of the meteorite find: Grovers Mill, New Jersey, the fictional site where a Martian space ship touched down in the famous radio play "War of the Worlds," which sparked widespread panic when it was aired.

Another tipoff was the mysterious ailment that sent researchers into isolation at a hospital after they discovered the bowling-ball-sized meteorite at the mouth of a naked mole rat burrow. They experienced "flu-like symptoms," but analysis of the meteorite provided even more alarming news: the rock was reportedly harbouring the ebola virus.
For U.S. television viewers, the lab technician's name gave the joke away. It was Dana Sculley, a character on "The X-Files" programme about UFOs and conspiracies.

Doubters who continued to read the Web page might have agreed with a sceptic quoted near the end, who said the meteorite's chemical composition was not unlike that of a component of asphalt used in the Eisenhower administration.
"This could very well be a chunk of the New Jersey Turnpike," the site quoted one doubter as saying.
The Science hoax was put together by Richard Stone, who prepares the magazine's Web site.
"Science is a beacon of strong scientific journalism and accuracy, but we do have a playful side," Stone said in a telephone interview. He said he laboured to make sure everybody got the joke.
"We just wanted to make sure that we had enough clues in the story," he said. "We had a ton of clues, especially for scientifically literate people."

Even scientific illiterates would have figured it out if they clicked on what was supposed to be an image of the rock: what showed up then was a cartoon of a smiling bowling ball and the words "Happy April Fools!"

Most responses to the joke were positive, Stone said, but, "We had a couple people who weren't happy we ran with a fictional story. They view Science as ... the source of scientific news and they felt that they didn't want us to branch off."
